Sendust particles used are composed of 5% Al, 10% Si, and 85% Fe.
Two average particle sizes were studied: approximately 5 µm and 20 µm.
Volume ratios of sendust in polystyrene resin ranged from 20 to 40 vol%.
Optimal volume ratios for maximum absorption bandwidth are ~30 vol% for 5 µm and ~35 vol% for 20 µm particles.
Return loss below -20 dB corresponds to 99% absorption of incident electromagnetic power.
The composite with 5 µm particles achieved a normalized -20 dB bandwidth of approximately 27%, much larger than commercial absorbers (~10%).
Absorption frequency bandwidth broadens with increasing volume ratio up to the optimal point.
The absorber thickness that maximizes return loss decreases as the volume ratio of sendust increases.
The frequency dependence of relative complex permeability µ* is governed by natural magnetic resonance and eddy currents.
Eddy currents reduce µ′ below 1 at frequencies above 10 GHz.
The Maxwell–Garnett effective medium model was used to fit the effective permeability of the composite.
The frequency dependence of µ* includes contributions modeled by Debye (domain wall motion), Lorentz (spin motion), and eddy current terms.
Samples were hot-pressed at 5 MPa and cooled naturally before shaping for measurement.
Measurements were conducted from 0.1 to 20 GHz using a vector network analyzer with full two-port S-parameter method.
The composite absorber contains no rare metals, making it low-cost.
Denser packing of 20 µm particles leads to higher permittivity and lower absorption frequency compared to 5 µm particles.
Spin resonance effects appear above 1 GHz and contribute to absorption bandwidth improvement.
The study confirms that controlling particle size and volume ratio allows flexible design of electromagnetic wave absorbers.
The non-reflective condition is used to calculate ideal µ′ and µ″ values for zero reflection.
The composite with 5 µm particles satisfies the non-reflective condition approximately between 10 and 16 GHz at 2–3 mm thickness.
